newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti says H1 figures all in order.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti says H1 figures all in order.

text.p: Italy's troubled information technology group Olivetti on Friday refuted criticism of its accounting practices and said that its first-half 1996 figures published this week were "rigorously" in order.

Earlier this week, Renzo Francesconi, the company's former director-general in charge of finance, administration and auditing, had alleged the figures published on Tuesday were misleading and this prompted a stock market watchdog inquiry.

An Olivetti statement, published a day after a three-and-a- half hour meeting with bourse watchdog Consob in Rome on Thursday, said the first half results were drawn up in rigorous observation of current legal standards and accounting practices.

Olivetti confirmed that the group's net debt at the end of the half-year at June 30, 1996 was 1.261 trillion lire after 775 billion lire ($513.6 million) at the end of 1995, despite Italian newspaper reports that the debts could be much higher.

Consob said that Olivetti shares would resume trading on the Milan bourse on Monday after a two-day suspension as officials from the stock market watchdog met first with Francesconi and then with top Olivetti executives on Thursday.
"The rumours about the need for further provisions such as to significantly worsen the six-month results are completely unfounded," the Olivetti statement said.

When Olivetti published its first half results late Tuesday it showed sales slumping, debts deepening, continuing losses after five straight years in the red, and a 200 billion lire provision to streamline parts of its loss-making businesses.

Olivetti said the 200 billion lire charge was its best estimate of provisions needed to restructure the company. It did not rule out further charges, but it said these were likely to be covered by sell-offs of "substantial activities" from the company. It gave no details in the statement.

A Consob spokesman said that the watchdog had not made a full and detailed examination of Olivetti's first-half figures, but had made enough enquiries to allow the re-listing of the shares on Monday. Consob said it would continue to monitor the financial accounts of the company, which will include requesting the opinion of the Olivetti's internal auditors.

Francesconi resigned from Olivetti on Wednesday after only six weeks with the company he joined from State broadcaster RAI. He was brought in by new Olivetti chief executive Francesco Caio to repair the finances of the loss-making company.

Olivetti surprised the Italian stock market with a first half loss of 440.8 billion lire late Tuesday and said its chairman of 18 years and major shareholder Carlo De Benedetti was stepping down afer a reported boardroom clash with Caio.
The crisis comes at a time Olivetti is switching its focus away from its old core businesses of computers and office equipment towards the fast-growing markets of telephony.

But as the core businesses have started to falter from stiff competition, the new ones of mobile and fixed-line telephone networks are still absorbing cash and have yet to put in a profit. ($1=1509 Lire)
